title: Restoring an Old Radio
story:
The radio had belonged to Marco Benedetti's grandfather, and for years it had sat silent beneath a layer of dust. Marco had always intended to restore it, although he knew little about valves, capacitors, or the patient work of soldering. One wet Saturday he carried the wooden case into the kitchen, spread a cloth over the table, and removed the back panel with a borrowed screwdriver. The components were smaller and more delicate than he had expected. However, a diagram glued inside the lid still showed where each wire belonged, and that diagram gave him more confidence than any instructions he had watched.

He cleaned the dial first, because the numbers were cloudy and he wanted one visible sign of progress. Although several screws were rusted, they turned eventually, and the speaker cloth, which had sagged, could be tightened with a needle and strong thread. His sister Giulia looked in twice to ask whether the kitchen would smell of hot plastic, and he promised to stop if anything grew warm.

By evening the case was empty and the table was covered with neat rows. Marco felt proud and slightly alarmed, since taking an object apart is easier than persuading it to work again. He reheated the dull joints, replaced one cracked capacitor from a specialist shop, and checked every connection against the diagram. However, when he switched the set on, there was only a faint hum and a smell of warm dust.

The next morning he noticed a loose wire behind the tuning knob. He soldered it again, more carefully, and switched the radio on with the volume low. A voice came through the static, thin but unmistakable, reading a weather bulletin as if the set had never been silent. Marco laughed, then lowered the volume so that the voice would not wake Giulia. The repair was far from perfect, although the old radio had found its way back into the life of the house.

The neighbour who lent a screwdriver
His grandfather
